name: Phosphatidylserine
lead: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a glycerophospholipid found in all cell membranes, most abundant in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane and enriched in the brain, where it makes up roughly 13 to 15 percent of cortical phospholipids. [2] It is also sold as an oral dietary supplement, usually derived from soy lecithin, marketed for memory and cognition, and in sports and recovery products for exercise stress. [2][1]

In appearance-focused communities PS is used mainly as a recovery and stress supplement. Lifters describe taking it to blunt cortisol around hard training or poor sleep so they can recover, train more and hold on to muscle, and some take it in the evening to wind down; the chain runs from calmer stress response to better sleep and recovery to more productive training and a better physique.[13][14][15][16]

In 2003 the US FDA allowed a qualified health claim for PS and cognitive decline, noting the supporting research was limited and preliminary, while the European Food Safety Authority in 2010 concluded that cause and effect had not been established for several PS claims, including stress reduction. [2] Clinical trials have studied PS in older adults, children with ADHD and athletes. [3][4][5][6][7][17][18] No trial has measured appearance outcomes.

paras: PS has two fatty acids esterified to glycerol and a phosphoserine head group. Plant- and animal-derived PS differ in fatty acid composition. In mammals it is made in the endoplasmic reticulum by head-group exchange from phosphatidylethanolamine or phosphatidylcholine. [2]

In the cell it stays almost entirely on the inner face of the plasma membrane. It provides docking sites for signalling proteins such as Akt and protein kinase C, associated with neuronal survival and synapse formation, and a 2015 review describes it as required for healthy nerve cell membranes and myelin. [2][8][9][19] During apoptosis PS flips to the outer membrane and acts as an 'eat-me' signal for phagocytes, which underlies the widely used annexin V assay. [2][8][9]

Meat and fish are the main dietary sources, with soy lecithin and white beans among plant sources, and the average Western diet supplies about 130 mg a day. [2] Early supplements were extracted from bovine brain; concerns about bovine spongiform encephalopathy in the 1990s moved manufacturers to soy-derived PS, and some products now use sunflower lecithin. [2] PS is sold as capsules and in multi-ingredient sleep, nootropic and 'cortisol' products. [10]

In May 2003 the FDA allowed a qualified health claim that PS may reduce the risk of dementia and cognitive dysfunction in the elderly, with a required statement that the research is very limited and preliminary; the agency said qualified experts did not agree a relationship exists, and the claim applies to soy-derived products. [2] In October 2010 an EFSA panel found no established cause-and-effect relationship for claims on memory and cognition in the elderly, mental health or stress reduction, reasoning that bovine and soy PS may differ. [2]

A 2001 trial of soy-derived PS in elderly people with age-associated memory impairment found no significant effect on cognitive performance at 6 or 12 weeks. [2] A 2010 Japanese study of soy PS reported improved memory in elderly people with memory complaints, and later reviews suggest a possible benefit in mild cognitive impairment, though the mechanism is unclear. [2] A 2015 review of 127 articles concluded that PS is absorbed, crosses the blood-brain barrier and supports memory-related functions, a stronger reading than the FDA's. [19]
No study has examined PS for facial appearance, body composition or other looksmaxxing outcomes, and the EFSA's 2010 opinion did not accept a stress-reduction claim. [2]

A 2002 safety report judged 200 mg three times daily safe in elderly people. [2] The FDA's qualified health claim applies to soy-derived products. [2] Supplement labels warn consumers about product-specific issues such as not ingesting included desiccant packets. [10]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, PS appears in several roles. In 2004 a poster suggested a 'cortisol blocker like phosphatidylserine' for someone under physical and psychological stress, [14] a 2010 thread on muscle loss after a rave lists it with glycine and vitamin C as a cortisol-lowering supplement, [15] and a 2024 training log plans 'cortisol blockers (phosphatidylserine-based)' alongside creatine to build muscle. [16] Others use it for sleep and relaxation: a poster on testosterone therapy advises taking it with magnesium glycinate near bedtime, [13] and a 2012 thread lists it with L-theanine and bacopa as a calming supplement. [20] A 2019 log lists it in a pre-workout stack. [21] Another poster calls it 'great for memory'. [22]

Registered and published human studies of PS cover cognition in healthy children aged 8 to 12 (208 participants), ADHD in children (including a trial combining PS with omega-3 fatty acids), mild cognitive impairment, cognition in older adults, familial dysautonomia, cycling time-trial performance and eSports performance. [3][4][5][6][7][11][12] A randomised trial of soy PS in 36 children with ADHD examined memory and symptoms, [17] a 2025 randomised trial tested a PS-containing supplement in Chinese older adults with mild cognitive impairment, [18] and a 2024 randomised trial tested PS enriched with omega-3 in children and adolescents with epilepsy and ADHD. [23] Results for several of the registrations are not summarised in the registry records, and none addresses appearance.

lore.intro: In T Nation discussions PS is mostly described as a cortisol-blocking or relaxation supplement, and sometimes as a memory aid.[14][15][16][13][22]

claims.claim: PS lowers cortisol and protects muscle during stress or hard training
claims.believers: Posters recommend it as a 'cortisol blocker' for stress, rave weekends and muscle-building phases.[14][15][16]
claims.experts: The EFSA found in 2010 that cause and effect was not established for PS claims including stress reduction;[2] no trial has examined PS for muscle outcomes in these communities.

claims.claim: PS taken near bedtime helps relaxation and sleep
claims.believers: A TRT forum poster suggests taking it with magnesium glycinate close to bed to help the body relax.[13]
claims.experts: Published PS trials have studied cognition and ADHD rather than sleep.[3][4][5][17]

claims.believers: A poster calls it 'great for memory'.[22]
claims.experts: A 2001 trial found no effect in older adults; later studies and a 2015 review report possible benefits, and the FDA's 2003 claim carries a limited-evidence statement.[2][19]

card.summary: Membrane phospholipid sold as a memory and recovery supplement; trials are mainly in cognition, none for appearance.
card.note: FDA health claim is qualified as limited and preliminary; EFSA found no established cause and effect.

quick.overview:
Phosphatidylserine is a fat-like molecule found in every cell membrane and concentrated in the brain. Supplements, now usually soy-derived, are sold for memory and recovery.

Human trials have mostly looked at cognition in older adults, children and athletes. None examine appearance outcomes, so its looksmaxxing role rests on supplement marketing.
quick.mechanism: PS helps anchor signalling proteins in neuron membranes and tags dying cells for removal by immune cells. How oral supplements might affect brain function is not settled.
quick.risks: A 2002 safety report found a daily regimen safe in elderly people. Supplements are unregulated products, and the FDA's 2003 health claim carries a disclaimer that the evidence is limited.

chain: Taken around training or in the evening
Marketed to blunt stress hormones and aid relaxation
Easier recovery and sleep, supporting more training
angle.text: Lifters in forums describe PS as a cortisol-lowering recovery aid taken after training or before bed, with the aim of protecting muscle and recovery capacity. Trials of PS have focused on cognition and mood rather than muscle or appearance.
